reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Jayden turned four today. His family had a party at the park. There was cake, juice and balloons. Mom set the cake down. Jayden counted the candles. "One, two, three, four." He asked Mom, "Why four candles?" Mom said, "You are four, so we put in four." He smiled big.

Grandma held up paper letters. "Can you spell your name, Jayden?" He did it slow. "J, A, Y, D, E, N." Grandma taped the letters to the table. Then the wind came. The wind blew out two candles. Jayden asked, "Who blew them out?" Dad said, "The wind did. The wind can blow out candles too." So Jayden covered the candles with his hands. Mom lit the two candles again. They stayed lit.

Everyone sang the birthday song. Jayden made a wish. He took a big breath and blew. All four candles went out at the same time. His friends clapped. Then a small surprise ran up. It was the park duck. It sat right by the cake. "Hello, duck," Jayden said. "You cannot eat my cake." He gave it a little bread bit instead.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Peyton ran to the park. She wanted to find the ice cream truck. Where was it?

Peyton closed her eyes. She could not see the truck. But she could hear it! Her ears heard a little bell. Ding, ding, ding! "The truck is coming!" she said. She used her ears.

Peyton's nose sniffed the air. Her nose smelled something sweet. It smelled like vanilla! She opened her eyes. Now her eyes could see the big white truck. It was by the black fence at the end of the yard. She ran and ran.

Peyton held the cold cone with her hands. Her hands felt the cold. She took a lick. Her tongue tasted the sweet, sweet cream. "Yum!" said Peyton. "My ears found it first!" The bell rang again. Ding, ding, ding!

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story: Maeva went to the store with Dad. The store had food, toys, and a little book corner. Maeva saw a book with a fish on it. The fish could swim in deep blue water. She opened the book. There were little marks on every page. "What are these little marks?" she wondered. Dad said, "Those are words. Words tell you things." Maeva turned the pages one by one. Front to back. Page one, page two, page three. Then she got to the end. The fish went deep down and hid. "I want to keep this book forever," said Maeva. Dad shook his head. "This book is from the library. We borrow it. We take it home, then bring it back. Other kids read it too." A big clock ticked on the wall. "The clock tells us when to bring it back," said Dad. Maeva held the book tight. She looked at the fish one more time. "Okay," she said. "But can we read it at home first?"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Athena ran to her cubby at daycare. Her bunny was not there. Bunny was her favorite toy. She looked in the coat pile. No bunny. She looked under the snack table. No bunny.

Teacher Sam knelt down beside her. "Where did you play last?" he asked. Athena thought hard. "The sand table," she said. "First I played there. Then we went outside." So she went back to the sand table. She dug with both hands. Sand went everywhere. Still no bunny.

Then Athena looked at her shoes. They were full of sand. "I put on my boots to go outside," she said. "I had to cut my playing short for winter." Outside, the snow was crunchy under her feet. She walked in her old boot prints. Step by step. Crunch, crunch. Then she saw it. Bunny's ear was sticking out of a snow pile by the sleds.

"Bunny!" said Athena. She hugged him tight. Teacher Sam smiled. "You found him by going back where you were." Athena nodded. "Bunny fell in the snow when I built the pile." She put bunny in her pocket. Then she ran back inside to show her friends.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Isaiah held Mama's hand at the store. "We need apples," said Mama. "And we must not forget the juice."

Isaiah loved the store. The aisles were so long! First they passed the toy aisle. He saw a red truck and a fuzzy bear. Then they passed the fish tank. Little fish swam round and round. "Fish are animals," said Isaiah. "Yes," said Mama. "Fish are animals that swim."

At last they found the apples. Isaiah picked one up. It was round like a ball. He put it on the edge of the cart. The apple rolled! It rolled because it was round. Round things roll! The apple dropped down, down, down.

Mama caught it. She laughed and laughed. "Round apples need the bag," she said. Isaiah put the apple in the bag. It could not roll there. Then Mama held up the juice. "We did not forget!" Isaiah clapped his hands. "Apples, juice, fish, and my truck!" said Isaiah. "Best store day ever!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma came to stay at Amira's house. "How long is a week?" Amira asked. Grandma said, "Seven sleeps." So every morning, Amira dropped a stone in a jar. One stone, two stones, three stones. "Each sleep makes one stone," she said. That was the rule.

Amira wanted Grandma to sleep well. She gave her a soft blanket to keep her warm. But at night, Amira heard a bump. Grandma could not sleep. "Was the blanket too small?" Amira wondered. No, Grandma had bumped her toe on the dark path to the bathroom.

So Amira found her toy sheep. It was white and soft. She set the sheep by the bathroom door. "Now you can see where to walk," she said. Grandma patted the sheep. That night there was no bump. The little sheep glowed in the dark, and the path was clear.

Four stones, five stones, six stones, seven stones. The jar was full. Grandma gave Amira a big hug. "You kept me warm and safe all week," she said. Amira held up the sheep and smiled. "The sheep did it too."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Leah sat in her car seat. The car went fast, then it went slow. "One red car. Two blue cars. Three trucks," she said.

She wanted her water bottle. It was in the deep pocket by the door. She could not reach it. "Daddy, please help me," she said. Daddy reached back and got it. "Thank you," said Leah.

Then the car had to swing around a big corner. The bottle tipped over. Water dripped on the seat. "Oh no," said Leah. "The bottle fell because the car went around the corner." Daddy said, "Sorry, Leah. I will go slower." He found a towel and wiped the seat.

Then Daddy told her a joke. "What does a car say? Beep beep!" Leah laughed and laughed. "Tell it again, please," she said. Daddy smiled and started the joke one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Owen wanted the red truck at daycare. Ben had it. Owen grabbed it. Ben cried loud.

Miss Amy came over. She sat down by Owen. "Try asking," she said. Owen looked at the truck. "Can I have the truck, please?" he asked. Ben sniffed. "Okay. After I do one more beep."

Owen waited. He counted the beeps. One, two, three. Ben held out the truck. "Thank you," said Owen. It was windy outside the window. The tree tapped the glass, tap, tap. Owen pushed the truck on the rug. It bumped Ben's foot. "Sorry, Ben," said Owen. "It's okay," said Ben.

Then Owen could not find the truck ramp. He looked under the table. He looked in the box. He whispered to Miss Amy, "Can you help me?" She found the ramp behind the shelf. Owen pushed the truck down, down, down. "It goes fast because the ramp is tall!" said Owen.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Sophia sat at the dinner table. The lamp made a warm circle of light. Mama put down a bowl of soup. "Today we have soup," said Mama. "Yesterday we had pasta. Tomorrow we will have spaghetti." Sophia looked at her bowl. "I want spaghetti now," she said. "Spaghetti comes later," said Mama. "First soup, then spaghetti."

Sophia did not want to wait. She turned her spoon around and around. She shook her spoon and the soup went drip, drip, drip. One drop, two drops, three drops. The table got messy. Mama gave her a cloth. Sophia wiped one drop, two drops, three drops. The table was clean now.

"I want tomorrow now," said Sophia. Mama smiled. "Tomorrow comes after we sleep. Yesterday we had pasta. Do you remember?" Sophia thought. Yes, she remembered the pasta. It was gone. "Pasta was yesterday," said Sophia. "Soup is today." "That's right," said Mama. Sophia ate her soup, one spoon, two spoops, three spoons.

The bowl was empty. "Now soup is done," said Sophia. "Now it is spaghetti time," said Mama. She set down a plate of spaghetti. "Later came!" said Sophia. She lifted her fork and twirled the noodles around and around.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Olivia wants to paint a cat. But her cat is orange. She has no orange paint. She has red, yellow, and blue.

"Red, yellow, blue," she says. She taps each wooden cup. Those are her three paints. None of them is orange.

She stops. She has a question. Can two paints make a new paint? She dips her brush in red. She dips it in yellow too. She stirs them on her plate.

The paint turns orange! Olivia jumps up. "Red and yellow make orange!" she shouts. Now she can paint her cat.

She paints a big orange cat. Then she wonders about blue. She mixes red and blue next. The new paint is purple! "Wow," she whispers. Purple was hiding in her cups all along.

She runs to find her cat. "Look!" she says. The real cat sniffs the painting. Then he rubs his head on it. "You like orange too," Olivia says. She holds up her purple brush. "Next, I paint you a purple hat!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Mya sat on the playroom floor. She had ten red blocks. She wanted to build one big tower.

"Mom, come see my tower!" she called. Mom was feeding the baby. "One minute," said Mom. Mya counted her blocks to see how many she had. "One, two, three, five, eight," she said. She looked at the blocks left in the pile. Her count did not use them all up. Something was wrong.

Mya frowned. She tried again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." This time she tapped one block for each word. Every block got a word. No block was left out. "The numbers go in a row," she said. "They have a job. Each one taps one block." She remembered a song at school. It went the same way every time, one to ten.

Mom came in with the baby. "Show me," said Mom. Mya stacked and counted. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" The tower stood tall. The baby clapped her hands. "Look, baby," said Mya. "You can like my tower. It has ten blocks. Ten is lucky today."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Blake's bear was sick. He had a tummy ache from too many pretend cookies. "I will be the doctor," Blake said. She put a bandage on his tummy. She gave him pretend soup in a small cup.

Next, her bunny was hungry. Blake fed her a carrot that was really an old sock. Bunny chewed and chewed. Then Bunny felt much better.

"Now my job is done," said Doctor Blake. But then she heard a tiny sound. Peep, peep! She looked under her bed. Her doll was hiding there. "You need a house," said Blake. She made a house from a big box. She planted a feather in a cup to be a tree for the yard. The doll moved in and smiled.

Blake clapped her hands. "When I take care of you, you get happy," she said. Then the bear, the bunny and the doll all sat down with her for one more pretend cookie.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Leon was at Grandma's house. It was a snowy day. Big white flakes fell past the window.

"I will make pancakes for everyone," said Leon. Grandma stood close by. Leon mixed flour, milk and one egg. He poured a pancake into the pan. It made a happy sizzling noise.

But the pancake stayed flat and thin. It looked like a little snowy plate. Leon frowned. "Why won't it get big?" he asked. Grandma showed him the baking soda box, still on the shelf. "We forgot this," she said.

Leon added the baking soda to the bowl. He poured a new pancake. It sizzled again. Then it puffed up, big and fat! "It got big because of the baking soda," said Leon. Grandma smiled.

The family ate the big pancakes. Daddy ate four. "Leon made these," said Grandma. Leon held his warm plate and grinned.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Gabriel went to the park with Dad. The pond was still and quiet. Two ducks swam by and began to fish in the water. Dad put a big hoop on the grass. He gave Gabriel a small red beanbag.

"Throw it in," said Dad. Gabriel threw the beanbag very hard. It flew over the hoop and landed in the grass. He tried again, hard and fast. It bounced off the rim. Then Gabriel tried a slow, soft toss, low and easy. The beanbag went up and dropped right into the hoop.

"I threw it slow and it went in!" said Gabriel. Dad clapped. Next Dad rolled him a big blue ball. Gabriel held out one hand. The ball hit his fingers and fell. Dad rolled it again. This time Gabriel held out both hands, open wide. The ball landed right in them. He caught it!

"You used two hands," said Dad. Gabriel laughed. "One hand was silly," he said. He hugged the big ball. The sun made a bright window of light on the path. Gabriel walked home holding his ball all the way.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story: Wyatt wanted to find ten bugs for his jar. He only found one small brown bug on the porch. He sat down and felt sad. Then he heard Mom singing in the kitchen. She was counting spoonfuls of flour. "One, two, three," she sang. Wyatt tapped his knees. The words went in order, and they never stopped. So he started to sing too. "One, two, three, four," he sang. He walked to the garden. "Five, six, seven." He looked under a leaf. Two green bugs sat there! "Eight, nine." He peeked at a rock. A tiny red bug crawled past. "Ten!" said Wyatt. He had ten bugs now. "The song helped me look slow," he said. Mom came out and smiled. "Can I see your jar?" she asked. Wyatt held it up so she could see every small bug. "Ten friends," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Elizabeth had a toy bunny. She held it in her arms. "Bunny is hungry," she said. Elizabeth found a little carrot in the kitchen. It was a food, and foods are for eating. She put the carrot up to the bunny's mouth. The carrot just sat there. The bunny did not chew. The carrot did not get smaller.

Elizabeth tried again. She made munching sounds. "Bunny, eat!" she said. The carrot still did not go away. Her big brother Sam came in. He held their real cat, Max. Sam put a bit of fish on the floor. Max bent his head. Max chewed and chewed. The fish was gone.

Elizabeth looked at Max. Then she looked at her toy bunny. "Toys do not eat," she said. "Real animals eat." Sam smiled. "That's right," he said. "Your bunny is soft and quiet. Max is soft too, but Max has a tummy."

Elizabeth gave her toy bunny a gentle hug. She gave the bunny a kiss on its little nose. Then she looked out the window at the street. A real dog was walking by with its owner. "That dog eats too," said Elizabeth. "One day Max can have more fish," said Sam. Max licked his lips and purred very loud.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Paisley held her baby doll at school. The baby was hungry, but the bottle was lost. Paisley looked in the toy box. She looked under the little table. No bottle anywhere.

Then she saw a small yellow block. She held it to the baby's mouth. "Here is your milk," she said. The block was not a bottle. But in pretend play, it could be one. Tom saw her and grinned. He picked up a block too. "My baby wants milk too!" he said.

Next they made a road on the carpet for the pretend car. Tom drove the car. "A stinky skunk is on the road!" he cried. Paisley dug in the toy box. She pulled out a spoon. "Use this shovel," she said. "Dig him out of the way." The car zoomed past. The babies drank their milk. "All better," said Paisley.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Riley sat at the little blue table. Teacher Sam put out letter cards. Riley wanted to find the R card, because R is for Riley.

She picked up a card. It had two bumps and one stick. She turned it around. She turned it again. The card looked the same both ways. Riley put it down and waited. She looked some more.

Then she picked up the R card. It had one bump and two sticks. When she turned it around, it did not look the same anymore. "This one turns different," said Riley. Teacher Sam smiled. Riley held up the R. "R goes rrr," she said, like a big cat.

At dinner time, Riley found the R on her milk carton. She turned it around. It still said R. "R goes rrr," she told her milk. Then she took a big drink.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
David stood by the gate. His green hat was on his head. He waited for his mom. "Mom!" he called. She came with a big bag.

David wanted to go to the park. But his shoes made a squish sound. He had stepped in a puddle at school. His socks were wet. His toes felt cold. Mom sat down on the bench. She took out dry socks from the bag. She pulled off the wet socks. She put the dry socks on his feet. "Warm now," said David. "The wet socks made my toes cold. Dry socks make them warm."

Then Mom gave him a banana. She used a small knife to cut it into pieces. David ate them all up. He drank his water. He was not hungry anymore.

They walked to the park. David ran in the sand. He went down the slide. "We will go home soon," said Mom. "Then a warm bath. Then pajamas. Then bed." David slid down one more time. "Again!" he said. Mom smiled and held out her hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Sadie sat at the dinner table. She wanted the red jello. Mom said, "Not now. Later, after your peas."

Sadie looked at her plate. The peas were still there. "Is it later now?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Mom. "Now you eat. Later comes after now."

Sadie ate one pea. Then two. Then three. "Now?" she asked.

"Keep going," said Mom.

Sadie talked about her day while she ate. "Today I played in the sand. Yesterday I played in the rain. Tomorrow I want to paint with the color blue."

Mom smiled. "That sounds fun."

Sadie ate the last pea. The plate was empty. "Mom! Now it is later! The peas are gone, so it is jello time."

Mom put the red jello on the table. Sadie took a big bite. "Yummy," she said. "After now comes later. And after today comes tomorrow!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Charlie ran to the little table. Today he would write his name! Miss Mia put down a fat pencil.

Charlie grabbed it with his whole fist. He pushed hard on the paper. The pencil slid away. The letter C looked all wobbly, like a yucky worm.

"Try again," said Miss Mia. "Lay the pencil on your hand."

Charlie laid the pencil on his fingers. He pinched it with two fingers, like a little crab. Pinch, pinch, rest! He lifted his hand and put it back down. Pinch, pinch, rest!

Now the pencil stood up tall. Charlie drew the C. Then H. Then A. "C, H, A!" he shouted.

"You did it!" said Miss Mia. "Now keep going."

Charlie went on. R, L, I, E. The letters marched across the paper like cars on a road. Straight ones, round ones, all of them neat.

Charlie held up the paper. "My name! Look, my name!"

Miss Mia clapped. Charlie grinned and traced it again, pinch, pinch, rest.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Jayden was at Grandma's house. He wanted to build a picture of the garden. He found Grandma's paint pots on the big table.

"One red, one blue, one yellow," he said. He counted them again. "But no green." The grass in Grandma's garden was green. His picture needed green. Now he had a problem.

He painted a red flower. He painted a yellow sun. Then he tried the grass. He put blue on the plate. He put yellow next to it. He mixed them with his brush.

The paint turned green. "It made green," Jayden said. "Blue and yellow make green."

Grandma came to look. "That is nice green grass," she said.

"Not bad," said Jayden. He painted the long, long grass. It was green all the way to the fence.

"More blue," he said. He dipped his brush again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Amira wanted to set the table. Mama gave her a stack of cups. "We need six cups," said Mama.

Amira put out cups. She counted them. "One, two, three, five, six." She scratched her head. The cups looked wrong. There were only five on the table.

Papa came in. He was hungry and tired. "Can I have a cup of water?" he asked.

Amira counted again. She pointed at each cup. "One, two, three, four, five." One cup was missing! The counting words had to go in a row. If she jumped from three to five, the count got mixed up.

Amira got one more cup. She touched each one as she said the words. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Now there were six cups, just like Mama said.

Papa drank his water. "Thank you, Amira," he said. "This helps me a lot."

Amira smiled. Then she sang her new song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Mama clapped, and the whole kitchen felt warm.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story: Aurora sat at the dinner table. In the middle of her plate was warm soup. She was hungry, but she felt grumpy. "What is this soup?" she asked. Her grandma said, "Use your nose and find out." Aurora sniffed with her nose. "Mmm, it smells like carrots!" Then she touched the bowl with one finger. It was hot, so she pulled her hand back fast. Her ears heard the soup bubble. Her eyes saw orange dots floating on top. She took a little sip. "I can taste it!" she said. Then she held her nose closed and sipped again. Now she could not taste the carrots at all. "Why?" she wondered. She let go of her nose. The carrot taste came back. "My nose helps my tongue!" she said. She painted a big smile on her face with her spoon.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Mason lost his monkey. His soft, spotted monkey was gone.

"I want my monkey," said Mason. "Where can he be?"

Grandma said, "Think. Where did you play last?"

Mason played in the blanket fort. He crawled in. "Not here." He looked under the big chair. "Not here." He peeked behind the couch. "Not here." That was one, two, three places.

Then Mason stopped. He thought hard. "I was playing before my nap. I had my monkey then. I dropped him. So he is near my nap spot!"

Mason ran to the little bed. He looked down. There was a spotted paw! Under the blanket corner!

"My monkey! You were hiding near my bed," said Mason.

He hugged his monkey tight. "Found you, monkey. Found you."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Brooklyn went to the library with her dad. She wanted to find her own book. But she could not read yet. The letters looked like little squiggles.

Dad gave her a clue. He said, "Your name starts with B." Brooklyn looked at the shelves. She looked and looked. There was a red letter on a book. It had two bumps and one tummy. Dad said, "That is B. It says buh."

Brooklyn put her finger on the B. "Buh, buh, Brooklyn," she said. The letter B was at the front of her name! Now she knew one letter all by herself.

She found more books with B. Each one had the two-bump letter. "Buh," she said each time. Dad smiled and nodded.

One book had a picture of a rubber duck. The duck sat in a bath. Brooklyn hugged the book. "B is for bath," she said. Dad said, "Yes! Buh, bath."

The sun did shine in the window. It made the B on her book glow. Brooklyn carried the book to the desk. She gave the librarian her card.

"Buh, buh, Brooklyn," she said, very proud.

The librarian clapped softly. "Your B book," she said.

Brooklyn held the book tight all the way home.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story: Emile found a thick book at school. It was about big red trucks. He loved it. He wanted to keep it forever. He put it in his bag. Then Miss Ana held up a small paper flag. The flag was stuck in the book Emile took. "Whose book is this?" she asked. Emile gave it back. He saw words on the flag. "What do the words say?" he asked. Miss Ana pointed to each word. Emile followed her finger. The words said take it home, bring it back. "So the book can go home with me?" he asked. "Yes," said Miss Ana. "But you must bring it back. Other friends want to read it too." Emile hugged the book. He read page one first. Then page two, all the way to the end. "I will bring it back," he said. On Friday, he put the book in the box. His friend Tom took it next. Emile waved goodbye to the trucks.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Ava sat at the dinner table. Rain tapped on the window. "It is a stormy night," said Mama. Ava drank her milk. "Milk comes from a cow," said Ava. The dog sat by her chair. He looked up with big eyes. "You beg for my carrots," said Ava. She gave him one little piece.

After dinner, it was bath time. Ava wanted to keep her socks on. She stepped into the tub. Splash! Her socks got all wet. "Oh!" said Ava. She pulled them off. They dripped in her hands. "Socks get wet in the bath," she said. "Why is that?" Then she touched the water with her toes. Warm! The wet socks went in the basket.

Mama dried her with a big towel. Ava put on soft pajamas. She brushed her teeth and climbed into bed. "Did you like the warm bath?" asked Mama. "Yes," said Ava. "But no socks next time."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Blake was at Mia's house. Mia's mama put on a song. The song had a beat. Boom, boom, boom.

"Clap like this," said Mia. She clapped on the boom. Blake clapped too fast. She clapped all over. The beat got lost.

"Listen first," said Mia. "Then clap."

Blake sat very still. She heard the boom, boom, boom. She clapped on each boom. Clap, clap, clap. It matched!

"I did it!" said Blake. "The claps go on the boom!"

"Now sing with me," said Mia. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star."

Blake knew that one! She sang the words from her head. She did not lose them. It was easy!

Then Mia's mama brought a surprise. A soap that smelled like strawberries! "Wash hands, then snack," she said.

The song played again. Blake clapped and sang at the same time. "Again!" she shouted. "Again, again!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Grandpa had a book on the table. Felix picked it up. The cover said a word. "What does it say?" he asked. "It says Dinosaur," said Grandpa. Felix looked at the letters. "Can I spell it?" he asked. He pointed at each letter. D, I, N, O, S, A, U, R. Grandpa smiled.

Felix opened the front of the book. He turned the pages one by one. The pictures came in order. First the egg. Then the big dinosaur. The last page showed the moon.

"I want to keep this book forever," said Felix. Grandpa shook his head. "It is from the library. We take it back on Thursday. Then other kids can read it too." Felix held the book tight. Then he had an idea. He got a pencil and paper. "I will spell dinosaur myself," he said. The parrot in the cage was noisy, but Felix kept writing. "D, I, N, O," he said. At last he drew a big green dinosaur under the letters. "Now I have my own book," he said. "And on Thursday, the library gets yours."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Florence went to the library with her dad. She saw a book about a small gray mouse. "I want this one," she said. The cover felt smooth. The pages made a soft swish when she turned them.

Florence opened the book. She saw little black marks on every page. "Dad, what are those?" she asked. "Those are words," he said. "They tell the story." Florence pointed at the marks. She turned pages from the front to the back. "The mouse moved to a big red barn!" she said. She could follow the mouse all the way.

At the desk, a kind lady put the book in a bag. "You can take it home," she said. "Bring it back when you are done. Then other kids can read it too." Florence hugged the bag tight.

At home, Florence read the book four times. Then she read it again. "I want to keep it forever," she said.

The next day, they went back to the library. Florence gave the book to the lady. A boy was waiting there. He smiled and took the mouse book. Florence watched him hold it. "He gets to read about the mouse now," she said. She moved to the shelf and picked a new book. This one had a bear on it. "This one is special too," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Hudson sat at the kitchen table. He had a big ball of yellow dough. He wanted to make a bear. He patted the dough flat. He rolled little balls for ears. He pushed them on the head. One ear fell off. He pushed it on again. This time it stayed.

The bear had sleepy eyes. Hudson gave him a soft blanket of blue paper. "Now you can sleep," Hudson said. The bear sat still under the paper.

Hudson licked a bit of dough off his finger. He made a face. It was salty! "Mom, the dough is salty," he said. Mom smiled. "We put salt in it," she said. Hudson looked at his bear. "You are made of salt," he whispered. He patted the bear's head gently and tucked the paper in tight.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Avery went to the store with Dad. She wanted the red balloon by the door. But another girl was there. The girl was holding the last red balloon.

Avery felt her eyes get hot. "Dad, can I take it?" she asked.

"No," said Dad. "She had it first. She gets her turn. Then we can ask for the next one."

Avery waited. She watched the girl's mom pay. The girl let go of the balloon string and the balloon began to dance near the ceiling fan. It bobbed up and down.

Then a store man came with a whole box. "More red ones," he said. He gave one to Avery. It had a sharp point at the knot, so Dad tied the string twice.

"Why did she get one first?" Avery asked.

Dad said, "Because she was first in line."

Avery nodded. "First in line goes first," she said.

At the car, she held the string tight. Her red balloon bobbed beside her all the way home. "My turn came," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Wyatt ran to the freezer aisle. It was cold in there! His coat was in the cart. "I will put it on all by myself," he said. He pushed his arms in fast. One sleeve was wrong. His arm was stuck behind his back! He wiggled and giggled and pulled it out. Then the arm slid in the right way.

Now the zipper. Wyatt pulled it up. It did not move. He pulled again. Still no zipper! Then he looked down. The zipper side was not in the little slot at the bottom. He pushed it in. Click! It was in. He pulled the zipper up, up, up. It worked! "I did it, Mama!" he said.

Wyatt jumped and his tag bounced like a feather. "The zipper only works when it starts in the slot!" he said. He unzipped it. He zipped it again. "Let's go find the ice cream," he said, and he marched to the freezer door.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Miles was four years old today. His party was at the big park. Grandma put the cake on the table. The cake had four little candles. All his friends ran over to see.

"Wait!" said Grandma. "The candles are still lit."

Miles looked. The four little flames were still dancing. Grandpa held his hand. "Blow with me," said Grandpa. Miles took a big breath. He blew hard. The flames went out. Thin smoke curled up.

"Why do we blow them out?" asked Miles.

"So the wax won't drip on the cake," said Grandpa with a smile.

Then Mom called, "Ice cream first!" Miles saw the ice cream tub. It sat in the sun. It was soft and wet at the edges. "The sun is melting it!" said Miles. "The sun makes it melt because it is hot."

"That's right," said Mom. "So we eat it fast."

Everyone got a bowl. Miles licked his spoon. The cold ice cream tasted sweet. His dog, Biscuit, sat by his feet and begged for a taste. Miles giggled and patted his head. Then Mom cut the cake into pieces. Miles took the biggest one. "Happy birthday to me!" he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Maeve sat on the grass with Dad. The sports field was big and green. People sat all around on blankets. Maeve had a little flag with a sun on it.

She held the flag up high. "I can see the game," she said. Then a man behind them said, "Oh. I cannot see now." Maeve turned around. Her flag was in front of his face. The flag was high. His eyes were low. That was why he could not see.

Maeve pulled the flag down. The man smiled. "Thank you," he said. "Now I can see the players."

A player kicked the ball. The ball went into the net. The net moved. The referee blew his whistle. Everyone stood up and cheered. Maeve clapped and jumped. Her tummy felt happy and jumpy inside.

After the game, Maeve skipped to the car. She held her flag down low. "The flag is for later," she said. Dad laughed and took her hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Madelyn went to the library with her dad. It was a bright morning. Story time was in the big room. Madelyn wanted to sing the counting song with the other kids. But she did not know all the words. Her tummy felt wobbly. "I might get it wrong," she whispered. Dad held her hand. "Let's listen first," he said.

The teacher sang, "One, two, three, four, five." She clapped on each word. Then she sang, "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Madelyn listened hard. The words were like a train. Each word sat in its own spot. First came one, then two, then three. They never hid. They always marched in the same order.

The teacher sang it again. Madelyn clapped and sang too. "One, two, three, four, five." Her voice was not alone. The whole room sang with her. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" She got every word right.

The song stopped, and Madelyn laughed. "The numbers always go in a row," she told Dad. "So I can remember them." Dad gave her a hug. Then they picked three books to take home. "One, two, three," Madelyn counted, all by herself.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Charlotte went to the store with Dad. They needed apples for pizza night. Dad said, "We need red apples too."

Charlotte saw the apples. Some were red. Some were yellow. Some were green. Her baby brother Sam pointed at a green apple. He wanted it.

A lady was giving out little apple pieces to try. Charlotte tried a green piece. Her mouth went tight and sour! "Yuck," she said. Then she tried a red piece. It was sweet. Charlotte looked at Sam. She said, "Green is sour, Sam. Red is sweet." She put red apples in the bag. She picked one small red apple just for Sam.

At home, Dad put hot pizza on the table. Red apple slices sat in a bowl. Sam held his little red apple. He took a big bite and smiled. Charlotte gave him a hug. Dad said, "Good picking, Charlotte." Charlotte bit her hot pizza slice and smiled too. "Red apples for Sam," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story: Michael wanted a cookie before lunch. Mom said, "First wash your hands." Michael ran to the sink. He got his fingers wet and turned to go. "Wait," said Mom. "Soap too. Count to twenty." Twenty felt like a long time. Michael rubbed the soap on his fingers. It felt smooth and slippery. He counted, "One, two, three." Then he stopped. "This is too slow," he said. His big sister came in. She was watering the little plant on the windowsill. "Sing the birthday song," she said. "One song is almost twenty seconds." Michael sang, "Happy birthday to you." He scrubbed while he sang. The soap made white bubbles. He rinsed his hands under warm water. His fingers smelled like clean soap now. "The song made twenty seconds fast," said Michael. Mom smiled and handed him a cookie. Michael took a big happy bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Sadie sat in her car seat. She had a new puzzle with her. It was a puzzle of a red fire truck. She tried to fit a piece. It did not go in. She tried again. It still did not go in.

"Please help me, Daddy," said Sadie. Daddy reached back his hand. He held the piece the cool way, flat and slow. The piece went in. "Thank you, Daddy," said Sadie. She clapped her hands.

Then Sadie dropped the box. Pieces fell on the floor. "Sorry, box," said Sadie. She waited for the car to stop. The car stopped at a red light. Daddy helped pick up the pieces. One by one, they went back in the box. "The light was red, so the car stopped," said Sadie. Daddy smiled. Then the light turned green, and off they went.
